clothing.title: How to Check Clothing QC Photos Before Shipping
clothing.description: Read hoodie QC photos, compare pit-to-pit and sleeve measurements with a garment you own, and ask for the warehouse photo that resolves a sizing question.
clothing.intro: A hoodie can look exactly right in the warehouse and still be the one you never reach for. Perhaps the chest has room for a T-shirt but the sleeves stop short, or the seller measured the body from a different starting point. Pick a hoodie you already like, a tape measure and the order details before you open the QC album. You can now answer three practical questions. Did the warehouse receive your chosen variation? Does its cut suit how you intend to wear it? Which uncertainty, if any, merits another photo before shipping?

sections.heading: Match the garment to the order
paragraphs: Start with the order line and its selected options. A single listing can carry a pullover, a zip hoodie and several print designs under the same product ID. Write down the style, colour and size you chose. In the full front and back views, look for the details that distinguish that version, such as the pocket shape, drawcord, zip or back print. If the order contains two similar pieces, ask which warehouse item number belongs to each album. A correct label in a close-up helps only when you can connect it to the garment in the wider view.

Next, enlarge the neck label or size sticker. Compare the lettering with the selected size and look for any separate labels on the garment and its bag. If a bag says L and the sewn label says M, save both photos and ask for one frame showing the hoodie and its packaging together. A wash label can help distinguish two versions if the listing specifies different fabric compositions or care instructions. The readable label tells you what the maker printed. A warehouse photograph alone gives little information about how warm the fabric will feel, how much it will shrink, or whether a brand label is genuine.

sections.heading: Read the pit-to-pit measurement
paragraphs: Zip or button your reference garment as you would wear it, lay it face up on a flat surface and smooth the front without pulling the sides. Choose the two points where the sleeve meets the body beneath each arm. Run the tape in a straight line between them and note the width in centimetres. In the warehouse photo, look for the same points, the zero mark, the number at the far edge and the tape unit. A tape laid several centimetres lower can measure a different part of a tapered hoodie. If one endpoint disappears under the sleeve, there is too little information for a close comparison.

Size charts may show either the flat width or a circumference. If a chart explicitly calls for twice the flat chest width, a hypothetical 56 cm pit-to-pit measurement corresponds to 112 cm by that method. A chart giving body measurements describes the wearer and follows a different convention. Read the chart heading, diagram and size row before doing the arithmetic. When the listing gives just “chest” and the unit, ask the seller what its number represents. Keep the comparison between two garment widths if that is the only measurement you can verify. That convention also makes a useful note alongside the saved photo.

sections.heading: Check the length, shoulders and sleeves together
paragraphs: Choose one body-length method you can repeat. For example, measure from the shoulder beside the neckline to the bottom edge, with the hood clear of the tape. A reading taken from the back of the neck can differ because the neckline and shoulder start at different heights. Note whether the ribbed hem is included and whether the reference rests flat. A cropped body with a deep ribbed band can have similar total length to your favourite hoodie while sitting at a different height when worn. Compare the shape in the wide shot as well as the number against the tape.

For a conventional sleeve with a shoulder seam, record shoulder width from seam to seam and sleeve length from that seam to the cuff. A dropped shoulder moves the start of the sleeve down the arm. A shorter sleeve measurement on that design can still put the cuff in the same place. A raglan sleeve runs into the neckline, so request a neck-to-cuff view and repeat that measurement on your reference if the cuts are comparable. Check whether the cuff is folded back, especially on an oversized style. Mark an uncertain endpoint in your notes so it does not become a confident sizing claim later.

sections.heading: Inspect prints, seams and the parts you use
paragraphs: Check the main print in a full front view with the body straight and both shoulders spread evenly. Use a stable feature on the garment, such as the centre zip, to judge placement. The edge of the warehouse table makes a poor reference if the hoodie sits at an angle. A fold across a letter can look like a gap in the ink. Ask for a flat close-up if the same mark would bother you when wearing the hoodie. For embroidery, look at the edges and backing that are actually visible. You can judge a loose thread in focus more readily than the durability of the entire design.

Look at places that take strain when you wear the garment. Check where the pouch pocket joins the front, where the cuff joins the sleeve and where the hood meets the neckline. On a zip hoodie, compare the top and bottom of both front panels with the zip closed. If one side appears longer, check whether one hem edge is tucked underneath. A useful follow-up names the exact area and asks for the view needed to settle it. “Please lay the right pocket corner flat and photograph the stitching from above” gives a warehouse worker a much clearer task than “please check quality.”

sections.heading: Work through a hoodie comparison
paragraphs: Suppose your favourite hoodie measures 56 cm across the chest, 68 cm from the shoulder beside the neck to the hem, and 60 cm from the shoulder seam to the cuff. In an illustrative warehouse album, the tape shows 58 cm across the chest and 66 cm down the body, with both endpoints readable. If both garments were measured the same way, the new one has 2 cm more flat chest width and 2 cm less body length. Hold the tape against your reference to see where that shorter hem would land. Decide whether you welcome the wider, shorter cut for the outfits you intend to wear.

Now imagine the sleeve tape ends at 58 cm but its starting point is hidden by the hood. Record the chest and length comparison and leave the sleeve open. If you often struggle with short sleeves, a clear shoulder-to-cuff photo is worth asking for. If both hoodies have different shoulder construction, a matching neck-to-cuff photo might answer your question better. Someone wearing a close-fitting jacket over the hoodie may care more about the added chest width. Your own reference and intended use determine which difference needs attention. These figures illustrate the method and say nothing about a particular listing or its labelled size.

sections.heading: Ask for one decisive view before shipping
paragraphs: In the order conversation, include the specific warehouse item, colour and size. For a missing chest reading you can send this wording. “Please lay my hoodie flat with the zip closed and the fabric relaxed. Measure straight across from one underarm seam to the other in centimetres. Please take one photo from above showing the whole tape, including zero and the opposite edge.” If your question concerns the sleeve instead, replace the measurement sentence with the two exact endpoints you used. Keep a copy of the original photo so you can compare the angle and see whether the follow-up answered your question.

Before choosing what to do, write a short note with the observations you can stand behind. “The sewn size matches, the chest is 2 cm wider than my reference, and the hem will be shorter” is enough to inform a decision. If those details suit you, use the shipping controls available on the order. If a critical measurement remains unreadable, ask for that view while the item is still accessible. A confirmed wrong size, missing piece or visible open seam calls for checking the available options and deadlines with the agent. Keeping the item number beside the photos makes it easier for the warehouse to act on the right hoodie.

bags.title: Will It Fit? How to Read Bag Measurements in QC Photos
bags.description: Check a bag’s usable opening, interior, strap drop and hardware in warehouse QC photos. Work through a phone and notebook example before shipping.
bags.intro: Your notebook fits inside the rectangle drawn on a bag listing. Can you get it through the zip? Can you do that with a phone and keys already inside? A useful bag QC starts with the thing you most need to carry. Put that object on the table, measure it in its usual case or cover, and look at how you normally take it out. Then open the photos of the bag received for your order. The opening, lining and handle can each change how useful the bag will be, even when the outer measurements match the listing.

sections.heading: Identify the bag and what needs to fit
paragraphs: Write down the ordered size, colour, closure and strap option. Check the front, back and side photos against those choices. Small and medium versions can look deceptively similar when shown alone on a warehouse table. Count the handles, look for the clips for the removable strap, and check whether the version you chose has a divided interior. A partition that makes a bag convenient for a phone can prevent a notebook from using its full depth. If a strap or pouch was part of your order, find it in a wide view or ask whether it is inside the bag.

Measure the objects you carry in their actual form. Record a phone’s length, width and thickness with the case on. For glasses, measure the case, including the hinge. For a notebook, include the cover overhang and spiral binding. If a tablet normally travels in a sleeve, use the sleeve as your reference. Decide which items must be accessible separately. You might be happy to rotate a notebook when you pack for the day, but dislike having to remove it whenever your phone rings. That distinction helps you decide whether to ask about the main compartment or the smaller pocket first.

sections.heading: Measure the clear opening at the closure
paragraphs: In a top view of a zipped bag, locate both ends of the opening with the zip fully open and the bag relaxed. Look for the remaining slider, folded panels at the ends and the points where the two sides still join. The clear distance through which an object can pass may be shorter than the visible zipper tape. Ask for a ruler or tape laid straight between those obstructions. Make sure its zero and far endpoint are visible in the same picture. You can then compare the usable span with the edge of your object that would enter the bag first.

The opening has depth as well as width. If the sides meet immediately beside a wide opening, a thick glasses case may catch at the corners. On a flap bag, check how far the flap lifts and whether side tabs pull the opening inward. With a drawstring style, look at the mouth when the cord is naturally open. If a structured bag has a frame, ask for a view at its normal open position. A worker should be able to show that position without forcing the hinges or stretching the leather. A second view from a slight angle can reveal an obstruction hidden behind the tape.

sections.heading: Read the base, gusset and usable interior
paragraphs: A side panel or gusset gives a bag depth. Work out where that depth is measured. A broad base may taper towards the zip, while a soft bag laid flat can fold its gusset inward. In a side view, trace how the panel changes from base to top. In a view from above, locate the internal divider and any zipped pocket. If you need room for a lunch box, ask about the narrowest part it must pass through and the floor space in the compartment where it will rest. Using the widest external measurements for all three dimensions can make a box appear to fit.

Ask for the inside height from the compartment floor to the closed zip line when you carry an object upright. This matters for a bottle, a long wallet or a notebook that might hold the closure open. An internal pouch stitched across the base can also limit usable floor space. A removable base insert may affect the measurement, so request the view with it in place if that is how you will carry the bag. Where the lining or construction makes a precise internal measurement difficult, label it as an estimate. Leave its degree of uncertainty visible in your notes when you make the comparison.

sections.heading: Try a notebook and phone comparison
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical notebook that measures 21 cm tall, 14.8 cm wide and 1.4 cm thick with its cover. The bag photo shows a clear opening of 16 cm. If you insert the 14.8 cm edge first, that leaves a nominal 1.2 cm across the opening. You also need enough front-to-back clearance for the cover and binding, and at least the notebook’s height in the intended upright position. Suppose a separate photo shows only 19 cm of inside height under the closed zip. Placing the notebook upright in that position would leave 2 cm above the closure line.

Could it go sideways? That orientation puts the 21 cm dimension along the interior width and changes how the notebook must turn after entry. Check the compartment’s length and depth before assuming that turn is possible. Now add a phone measuring 15.5 by 7.5 cm in its case. If the pocket opening measures 8 cm and you insert the narrow end first, the spare width is only half a centimetre. Seams, a raised case edge and your fingers may make the phone awkward to retrieve. You can rehearse the movement with a similar bag at home. A paper rectangle cut to the phone’s outline can test orientation, although it lacks the thickness of the case.

sections.heading: Check strap drop, attachments and everyday access
paragraphs: To compare how a shoulder bag hangs, measure the drop of a bag you already enjoy wearing. Support its strap naturally and measure vertically from the top edge of the bag body to the inside of the strap at its highest point. For an adjustable strap, note the hole or slider position. Ask for the same setup on the warehouse bag. Total strap length includes the path down both sides and sometimes the clips. A shoulder-drop comparison is usually easier when both photos use the same endpoints. If you wear the bag over a winter coat, try your reference bag over that coat as well.

Look where the load passes from the strap into the bag. A close-up can show whether a clip is attached to the intended ring, whether a tab is twisted and whether a stitch line has visibly opened. In the interior photo, follow the lining near the zip and check for loose fabric entering the slider path. Ask for one view with the bag open and the strap attached if you want to see whether the strap crosses the opening. Photos can show the attachment geometry and visible condition. For a stiff or sticking closure, ask whether the warehouse can check its normal movement under its handling rules.

sections.heading: Request a measurement and make the decision
paragraphs: A focused request might read, “For the small black bag on my order, please open the main zip normally and photograph a ruler in centimetres between the two usable ends of the opening. Please keep both ends of the ruler in frame. My notebook is 14.8 cm wide.” If you already have that measurement, ask the next question separately. “Please measure from the inside base to the closed zip line in the rear compartment, with the base insert in place.” Those instructions tell the worker which compartment matters and let you compare the reply with a measurement you can repeat at home.

Record what the evidence supports in language you would use when packing. “Phone fits through the pocket opening, notebook stands above the zip, strap drop matches my everyday bag” is more informative than a single yes or no. If the notebook is essential, compare another size or ask about the options available on the order. If you only carry a phone and keys, the same result might suit you. Keep the measurement photos with the item number and note any open question before shipping. That record will also help when you compare another bag whose listing gives the same outer width but uses a different closure.
